sources.title: Emily Warren Roebling (Q49902), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-20): English description 'US civil engineer, helped complete the Brooklyn Bridge (1843-1903)', instance of human, born 23 September 1843, died 28 February 1903, citizen of the United States, Korean label 에밀리 워런 로블링. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day: Emily Warren Roebling' by William B. Ashworth Jr. (23 September 2019; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: after her husband Washington Roebling, chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge, was struck by caisson disease (a first attack after the 1870 caisson fire, a second in 1872), he directed the project from home for the remaining eleven years; Emily took his dictated instructions to the assistant engineers, learned the engineering problems and their solutions, was treated on site as the chief engineer (his formal title), and used diplomacy to settle disputes among the oversight boards; the author says most scholars believe she was effectively in charge in the later years, and that before the 24 May 1883 opening she was given the honour of the first walk across and insisted the assistant engineers join her. The article says it does not describe any formal engineering study and that little more is known of her. Library history essay by a historian of science; short and popular, not peer-reviewed.

American Society of Civil Engineers, 'Emily Warren Roebling' (Notable Civil Engineers, History and Heritage section; read in full, no named author or date): second-youngest of twelve children, studied mathematics and science, married Washington Roebling in 1865; after his decompression sickness she took notes on what remained to be done, studied strength of materials, stress analysis, cable construction and catenary calculations, visited the site daily to relay his instructions, kept records and handled his correspondence, and rode across the bridge with President Chester Arthur at the 1883 opening, where Abram Hewitt praised her; she completed a law certificate at New York University in 1899, managed the building of the couple's Trenton house, belonged to the Daughters of the American Revolution and the Huguenot Society, travelled to Russia for the coronation of Nicholas II and to London in 1896, and served as nurse and construction foreman at a Montauk camp for soldiers returning from the Spanish-American War. Professional-society page, admiring; it presents the claim that many suspected she was the real intellectual force as rumour, and does not say how much of the technical work was hers.

Hugh A. Stewart, 'Roebling, Emily (1844-1903)', in Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). Reference-work biography that dates her birth 1844 (other sources 1843) and says she had no formal training and took a 'crash course' in engineering and calculus in 1872; it says she supervised construction for roughly eleven of the bridge's thirteen years as an unofficial chief engineer, dealt with contractors and suppliers (including an 1879 scandal involving the Edge Moor Iron Company), mediated disputes among trustees, escorted Ferdinand de Lesseps in 1880, and in 1882 defended her husband before the American Society of Civil Engineers when trustees tried to remove him (a claim, including that she was the first woman to address that society, that the other sources read here do not repeat); it quotes David McCullough that it was 'common gossip' she was the real mind behind the project, notes a newspaper claim that she may have written a lecture series with no proof, and concludes she was a conventional woman who took the work on from loyalty and family financial need. Single-author encyclopedia entry drawing on the McCullough and Weigold books.

Sarah Pruitt, 'How Emily Roebling Saved the Brooklyn Bridge', HISTORY (published 26 February 2024, updated 2026; read in full). Popular-history article: after 1872 she acted as her husband's nurse and private secretary, wrote his letters, kept his notebooks, reviewed plans, visited the site and met contractors and bridge officials (David McCullough's phrase: his eyes, legs and right arm); when her independence fed false rumours that he had lost his mental capacity she worked to keep him from being replaced as chief engineer; at a meeting with iron and steel contractors she helped resolve problems with their patterns, and a 1883 New York Times article reported their surprise at her knowledge; in 1899 she graduated with high honours from the Woman's Law Class of New York University and wrote a prize-winning article in the Albany Law Journal on equality for women in marriage; Erica Wagner is cited as saying the bridge might not have been completed without her and as objecting to the label 'first woman field engineer'. Journalism built on McCullough and Wagner, not independent archival work.

Sophia Dembling, 'Emily Warren Roebling: A Cornerstone in the Construction of the Brooklyn Bridge', National Trust for Historic Preservation (Saving Places, 17 December 2014; read in full). Magazine-style profile: her brother Gouverneur K. Warren raised her after their parents died and encouraged her interest in science; she acted as her husband's secretary, messenger and representative, visited the site daily, wrote the correspondence from the Roebling house, and (quoting McCullough) once drew a diagram to help a manufacturer understand a superstructure part; the article addresses and dismisses the rumour that she was the de facto chief engineer, notes that Washington kept his title despite late efforts to remove him, calls her a diplomat in the project's disputes and scandals, and describes the carriage crossing before the opening (the rooster detail is presented without a source) and Hewitt's opening-day tribute. Popular preservation-society article relying on McCullough.

John A. Stuart, 'The Confluence of Allegory and Technology in Gendered Public Space: Emily Roebling and the Construction of the Brooklyn Bridge', 84th ACSA Annual Meeting proceedings (Association of Collegiate Schools of Architecture, 1996; 7-page paper read in full). Scholarly paper working from the press clippings Emily Roebling kept in scrapbooks: quotes the New York World of 23 May 1883 (a man 'well acquainted with the family' says she applied herself to engineering and was able to assume the duties of chief engineer; mill representatives were surprised when she sat down with them and cleared up their patterns), the Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 25 May 1883 and an 1881 speech by Rossiter Raymond, and her 1898 letter to her son saying she had more brains than any two engineers and that the bridge would not have carried the Roebling name without her; notes that what her engineering education comprised and what her duties were have never been recorded, that an Edge Moor Iron Company letter of 28 October 1879 assured her of prices, that the press shaped her as a model of modest womanhood, and that her graduating essay 'A Wife's Disabilities' at the 1899 Women's Law Class commencement won a $50 award. Critical-feminist reading of how she was portrayed; the paper has typographical errors (it gives her death as 1907) and its own argument that she was suppressed from the record.

Richard Howe, review of Erica Wagner's 'Chief Engineer: Washington Roebling, The Man Who Built the Brooklyn Bridge', Gotham Center for New York City History blog (13 September 2018; read in full). Independent review of a 2017 biography of her husband: says Washington was chief engineer for nearly fourteen years and directed the last six years of construction as a house-bound invalid from 110 Columbia Heights, that his illness (the bends, from 1872) was in part unexplained and that Emily was not always convinced by his complaints, that Marilyn Weigold called Emily the bridge's 'surrogate chief engineer', and that she was 'absolutely integral' to its construction in Wagner's words; adds that she graduated from NYU's Women's Law Course in 1899 and wrote 'A Wife's Disabilities'. The reviewer is sceptical of great-man framings and notes that many assistants and workers built the bridge without equal credit. Review of someone else's book; a secondhand voice on her role.

Jay Serafino, 'Emily Warren Roebling, the Woman Who Helped Build the Brooklyn Bridge', Mental Floss (27 February 2018; read in full). Popular article citing McCullough, the New York Times (1883 and 1983) and the Roebling Museum: she graduated with top honours from the Georgetown Visitation Convent, excelling in science and algebra; she relayed Washington's orders to departments, acted as his 'eyes and ears' on site, reportedly sketched steel specifications for a mill's representatives, and lobbied successfully to keep him from being ousted over his absences; an 1883 New York Times article quoted a source saying she had 'filled his position as chief in engineering staff', while McCullough stresses she never formally replaced him; some people speculated that Washington gave her a larger role only because he was losing his mind. Popular secondary source, largely McCullough.

portrait.reason: HOLD (portrait). Best candidate: Carolus-Duran, Portrait of Emily Warren Roebling, oil on canvas, signed and dated 'Carolus-Duran./Paris 1896.', Brooklyn Museum 1994.69.1 (gift of Paul Roebling), likeness; the creator died in 1917, so copyright (life plus 70 years) has expired in the United States. Blocker is the holder's own conflicting reuse terms: the Brooklyn Museum Terms of Use (July 2024, read via Internet Archive) say images of works the museum believes to be in the public domain may be downloaded for limited non-commercial, educational and personal use only, and its Image Services page (read via Internet Archive, 2026-01) requires a request and quote for higher-resolution or commercial use; the item-level statement (older Open Collection record read via Internet Archive: no known copyright restrictions, 'you may download and use Brooklyn Museum images of this work' with credit, high-resolution files by paid request) is more permissive, so the holder's statements conflict. The live object page and terms return a Vercel bot-check (HTTP 429) and were not bypassed. Commons carries the museum-contributed copy under PD-Art but the holder's published terms are a reproduction restriction, consistent with the Roster65 and Roster66 precedent of holding when the holder's terms are non-commercial only. Alternatives checked and not usable: Library of Congress LC-USZ62-120162 (1953 copy of a photograph taken c. 1860-1880, creator unknown, rights field reads 'No information on creator or on reproduction rights found with the image, 1997', sitter identified only by a newspaper-morgue caption); RPI Roebling Collection photograph (rights reserved, permission required); Rutgers Roebling Family Papers photograph (non-commercial educational use only); Brooklyn Public Library items (HTTP 403, rights not readable). No other portrait was substituted.

ATTRIBUTION: limited_but_usable: the Brooklyn Bridge role is documented by many sources, but nearly all trace to David McCullough's 1972 book and Marilyn Weigold's 1984 biography, her education and duties were never recorded (Stuart), her husband kept the formal title, and credit between the spouses cannot be separated. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Linda Hall (full), ASCE (full), Stewart in Women in World History (full), HISTORY (full), National Trust (full), Stuart ACSA 1996 paper (full PDF), Gotham Center review of Wagner (full), Mental Floss (full). Britannica returned HTTP 403 and was not read; Wikipedia, Weigold and McCullough were not opened. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all; her own 1898 letter is quoted only through Stuart and is not used as support. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: birth 1843 (most) vs 1844 (Stewart); the 1882 ASCE address and 'first woman to address' claim only in Stewart; whether she earned a law degree (Atkins and Koth, not cited) or a certificate or class completion (society biography, History, Stuart); who first crossed and when (Stewart: led trustees across the planks in 1880; Linda Hall: honour of first walk before the opening; National Trust and Mental Floss: carriage with a rooster) so no first-crossing claim is carded (the society biography has her riding across with President Arthur whereas the National Trust article has Arthur crossing from Manhattan; neither is carded); Stuart says the formal chief engineer title never changed.
